s0003.literal: Shen Zhong; Yuan Bi; Liu Zhongwei; Lu Shancai; Wang Zhi; Wei Zai; younger clansman Hui
s0003.idiomatic: Shen Zhong; Yuan Bi; Liu Zhongwei; Lu Shancai; Wang Zhi; Wei Zai; younger clansman Hui

s0004.literal: Shen Zhong, styled Zhongshi, was a native of Wukang in Wuxing.
s0004.idiomatic: Shen Zhong, styled Zhongshi, was a native of Wukang in Wuxing.

s0005.literal: His grandfather Yue was Liang Special Grand Master.
s0005.idiomatic: His grandfather Yue had been Liang's special grand master.

s0006.literal: His father Xuan was Liang Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
s0006.idiomatic: His father Xuan was an attendant gentleman of the Yellow Gate under Liang.

s0007.literal: Zhong loved learning and had considerable literary skill; he began his career as Registrar to the Prince of Nanping of the Garrison Guard and Household Retainer to the Heir Apparent.
s0007.idiomatic: Zhong loved study and wrote well. He entered service as registrar to the Prince of Nanping of the garrison guard and as household retainer to the heir apparent.

s0008.literal: At that time Emperor Wu of Liang composed the Thousand-Character Poem, and Zhong wrote a commentary on it.
s0008.idiomatic: When Emperor Wu of Liang composed the Thousand-Character Poem, Zhong annotated it.

s0009.literal: He and Xie Jing of Chen commandery were summoned together to the Wende Hall; the Emperor ordered Zhong to compose a bamboo rhapsody; when it was finished he presented it; the Emperor praised it and replied by hand-edict: Editorial footnote marker 1. "Your literary style is light and graceful—you truly do no dishonor to your ancestor.
s0009.idiomatic: He and Xie Jing of Chen were summoned together to the Wende Hall. The emperor ordered Zhong to write a rhapsody on bamboo; when it was done he presented it, and the emperor praised it and wrote back in his own hand: [1] "Your style flows lightly—you truly do no dishonor to your ancestor.

s0010.literal: " The Duke of Dangyang, Xiao Daxin, was made Inspector of Yingzhou and appointed Zhong Recorder within the commandery limits.
s0010.idiomatic: " The Duke of Dangyang, Xiao Daxin, became inspector of Yingzhou and made Zhong his recorder within the commandery limits.

s0011.literal: Soon he was removed and made Recorder to the Prince of Xiangdong, Pacifier of the South.
s0011.idiomatic: He was soon transferred to recorder to the Prince of Xiangdong, pacifier of the south.

s0012.literal: He was promoted to Household Retainer in the Heir Apparent's palace, concurrently Regular Attendant.
s0012.idiomatic: He rose to household retainer in the heir's palace and was concurrently made regular attendant.

s0013.literal: On embassy to Wei he returned and was made Adviser to the Prince of Luling of the Flying Cavalry and kept his post as retainer.
s0013.idiomatic: After an embassy to Wei he was made adviser to the Prince of Luling of the flying cavalry, retaining his post as retainer.

s0014.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion Zhong memorialized Emperor Wu of Liang, saying that the righteous household troops his family had long commanded were all in Wuxing, and asked to return to recruit them to attack the rebel; Emperor Wu approved.
s0014.idiomatic: During Hou Jing's rebellion Zhong memorialized Emperor Wu of Liang, saying the loyal household troops his line had long commanded were in Wuxing, and asked leave to return and raise them against the rebel. The emperor agreed.

s0015.literal: When Jing besieged the Terrace City, Editorial footnote marker 2. Zhong led his clansmen and volunteer followers—more than five thousand men—to reinforce the capital, encamped at Little Ferry, and drew up battle lines opposite the rebel Eastern Mansion; his army's bearing was very orderly, and Jing deeply feared him.
s0015.idiomatic: When Jing besieged the Terrace City, [2] Zhong led his kinsmen and volunteer followers—more than five thousand men—to relieve the capital. He encamped at Little Ferry and formed ranks opposite the rebels' Eastern Mansion. His troops were tightly arrayed, and Jing feared him greatly.

s0016.literal: From within the city Emperor Wu of Liang remotely appointed Zhong Right Commandant of the Heir Apparent's Guard.
s0016.idiomatic: From within the city Emperor Wu of Liang appointed Zhong right commandant of the heir's guard by remote commission.

s0017.literal: When the capital fell, Zhong surrendered to Jing.
s0017.idiomatic: When the capital fell, Zhong surrendered to Jing.

s0018.literal: When Jing was pacified, Zhong went west to Jingzhou; Emperor Yuan of Liang made him Household Retainer to the Heir Apparent and Grand Arbiter of his native province.
s0018.idiomatic: After Jing was suppressed, Zhong went west to Jingzhou. Emperor Yuan of Liang made him household retainer to the heir apparent and grand arbiter of his native province.

s0019.literal: Soon he was promoted to Left Chief Clerk of the Secretariat.
s0019.idiomatic: He was soon promoted to left chief clerk of the Secretariat.

s0020.literal: When Jiangling fell he was taken captive by Western Wei; soon he escaped and returned; Emperor Jing of Liang under the provisional regime appointed him Censor-in-Chief.
s0020.idiomatic: When Jiangling fell he was captured by Western Wei, but soon escaped. Emperor Jing of Liang, under the provisional regime, made him censor-in-chief.

s0021.literal: In the first year of Shaotai he was made Palace Attendant and promoted to Master of the Left for the People.
s0021.idiomatic: In the first year of Shaotai (555) he was made palace attendant and promoted to master of the left for the people.

s0022.literal: When the Founder received the Mandate, Zhong was made Director of the Secretariat, grand arbiter unchanged.
s0022.idiomatic: When the Founder took the throne, Zhong was made director of the Secretariat, retaining his post as grand arbiter.

s0023.literal: Because Zhong was renowned in the Founder's home region, the Founder greatly respected him, favored him with generous gifts, and treated him above his contemporaries.
s0023.idiomatic: The Founder, knowing Zhong's name in his own country, honored him deeply, heaped gifts on him, and favored him above his peers.

s0024.literal: Zhong was by nature miserly; inwardly he built up estates, and his wealth in coin and silk ran to hundreds of millions, yet he shared nothing with others.
s0024.idiomatic: Zhong was miserly by nature. He amassed estates at home until his wealth in coin and silk reached hundreds of millions, yet gave nothing away.

s0025.literal: He supported himself very meagerly; at court assemblies his clothes were often torn, and sometimes he carried his own cap and shoes.
s0025.idiomatic: He lived on almost nothing. At court his robes were often in tatters, and sometimes he carried his own cap and shoes.

s0026.literal: In the second year of Yongding he was concurrently made Minister of Works for Construction and supervised the building of the Hall of Supreme Ultimate.
s0026.idiomatic: In the second year of Yongding (558) he was concurrently made minister of works for construction and oversaw the Hall of Supreme Ultimate.

s0027.literal: He always wore a cloth robe and straw sandals, used hemp rope for a belt, and carried dried fish and vegetables for his lone meal; court gentlemen together mocked his conduct.
s0027.idiomatic: He always wore a cloth robe and straw sandals, bound himself with a hemp cord, and ate dried fish and vegetables alone. The gentlemen at court mocked him for it.

s0028.literal: Editorial footnote marker 3. Zhong was by nature narrow and quick-tempered; thereupon in resentment he went through the ranks slandering the dukes and ministers and reviling the court.
s0028.idiomatic: Editorial footnote marker 3. Zhong was narrow and hot-tempered. Stung by the mockery, he turned on the court, slandering dukes and ministers and reviling the government.

s0029.literal: The Founder was greatly angered; because Zhong had long enjoyed a fine reputation, he did not wish to execute him openly; later, on a leave to return to Wukang, he was ordered to take his own life in Wu, aged fifty-six.
s0029.idiomatic: The Founder was furious. Because Zhong still enjoyed a fine name, he would not kill him openly; later, when Zhong took leave to return to Wukang, he was ordered to die by his own hand in Wu. He was fifty-six.

s0030.literal: Yuan Bi, styled Wenyang, was the younger brother of Left Grand Master of the Golden Sigil Jing.
s0030.idiomatic: Yuan Bi, styled Wenyang, was the younger brother of left grand master of the golden sigil Jing.

s0031.literal: Upright and pure, with administrative capacity, of imposing stature, and careful in conduct.
s0031.idiomatic: He was upright and capable, tall in bearing, and scrupulous in conduct.

s0032.literal: He doffed the commoner's garb as Supernumerary Regular Attendant and served as aide in several princely establishments.
s0032.idiomatic: He left the commoner's dress for supernumerary regular attendant and served as aide in several princely households.

s0033.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion Bi wished to become a general.
s0033.idiomatic: During Hou Jing's rebellion Bi sought a military command.

s0034.literal: At that time Bi's elder brother Junzheng was Administrator of Wu commandery; Emperor Jianwen of Liang commissioned Bi as Leader of Direct Service in the Eastern Palace and ordered him to Wu to recruit soldiers.
s0034.idiomatic: At that time his elder brother Junzheng was administrator of Wu commandery. Emperor Jianwen of Liang commissioned Bi as leader of direct service in the eastern palace and sent him to Wu to raise troops.

s0035.literal: When Jing besieged the Terrace City, Bi led the men under his command to the relief.
s0035.idiomatic: When Jing besieged the Terrace City, Bi led his command to the relief.

s0036.literal: When the capital fell he withdrew to hold Dongyang; Jing sent troops in pursuit, and he went out by the eastern pass of Kuaiji through Tangcheng and attached himself to the Heir of Poyang, Xiao Fan.
s0036.idiomatic: When the capital fell he fell back to Dongyang. Jing sent troops after him; Bi slipped out by the eastern pass of Kuaiji through Tangcheng and joined the heir of Poyang, Xiao Fan.

s0037.literal: When Fan died, Bi thereupon surrendered to Jing.
s0037.idiomatic: When Fan died, Bi surrendered to Jing.

s0038.literal: When Jing was pacified, Wang Sengbian memorialized that Bi be made Administrator of Fuchun, concurrently Intendant of Danyang.
s0038.idiomatic: After Jing was suppressed, Wang Sengbian recommended Bi as administrator of Fuchun and intendant of Danyang.

s0039.literal: When the Marquis of Zhenyang usurped the throne, Bi was made Palace Attendant and sent on embassy to Qi.
s0039.idiomatic: When the Marquis of Zhenyang seized the throne, Bi was made palace attendant and sent as envoy to Qi.

s0040.literal: When the Founder received the abdication, Wang Lin held the upper reaches; Bi came from Qi with Liang's Prince of Yongjia, Xiao Zhuang, to Lin's camp.
s0040.idiomatic: When the Founder took the throne, Wang Lin held the upper Yangzi. Bi came from Qi with Liang's Prince of Yongjia, Xiao Zhuang, to join Lin.

s0041.literal: When Zhuang usurped the throne, Editorial footnote marker 4. Bi was made Palace Attendant and Chief Clerk to the Chancellor.
s0041.idiomatic: When Zhuang declared himself emperor, [4] Bi was made palace attendant and chief clerk to the chancellor.

s0042.literal: In the second year of Tiancheng, Bi with Lin escorted Zhuang to Zhakou; Lin's army was defeated; Editorial footnote marker 6. the troops all scattered; only Bi alone took a light boat and saw Zhuang to the northern border, entrusted Zhuang to Censor-in-Chief Liu Zhongwei, and had them enter Qi together; then he took leave and returned, came to the court to confess guilt, and Emperor Wen deeply approved his conduct.
s0042.idiomatic: In the second year of Tiancheng (561), Bi and Lin escorted Zhuang to Zhakou. Lin's army was broken; [6] the troops fled in all directions. Bi alone took a light boat, saw Zhuang to the northern frontier, and placed him in the care of censor-in-chief Liu Zhongwei to enter Qi together. Then he bowed farewell, returned, and presented himself to confess fault. Emperor Wen held his conduct in high esteem.

s0044.literal: Liu Zhongwei was a native of Niyang in Nanyang.
s0044.idiomatic: Liu Zhongwei was a native of Niyang in Nanyang.

s0045.literal: His grandfather Qiu in Qi times was summoned as Erudite of the National University and did not accept.
s0045.idiomatic: His grandfather Qiu, in Qi times, was summoned as erudite of the national university and declined.

s0046.literal: His father Zhi-lin was Aide in the Secretariat of Jing province.
s0046.idiomatic: His father Zhi-lin was an aide in the secretariat of Jing province.

s0047.literal: Zhongwei in youth had ambition and had read widely in letters and histories.
s0047.idiomatic: Zhongwei in youth was ambitious and had read widely in letters and histories.

s0048.literal: Under Liang's Chengsheng era he was Regular Attendant of the Secretariat.
s0048.idiomatic: Under Liang's Chengsheng era he was regular attendant of the Secretariat.

s0049.literal: Zhuang's false regime made him Acting Censor-in-Chief; he followed Zhuang into Qi and died in Ye.
s0049.idiomatic: Zhuang's puppet regime made him acting censor-in-chief. He followed Zhuang into Qi and died at Ye.

s0051.literal: Lu Shancai, styled Kongzhang, was a native of Wu in Wu commandery.
s0051.idiomatic: Lu Shancai, styled Kongzhang, was a native of Wu in Wu commandery.

s0052.literal: His grandfather Wengbao was Liang Director of the Water Office in the Ministry of Works.
s0052.idiomatic: His grandfather Wengbao was Liang's director of the water office in the ministry of works.

s0053.literal: His father Fan was Regular Attendant.
s0053.idiomatic: His father Fan was regular attendant.

s0054.literal: In the Shaotai era Commander Zhou Wenyu went out to garrison South Yuzhou; he did not understand documents, and so he took Shancai as Chief Clerk and entrusted all administration to him.
s0054.idiomatic: In the Shaotai era Commander Zhou Wenyu took up his post at South Yuzhou. Unable to manage documents himself, he made Shancai his chief clerk and left all administration to him.

s0055.literal: When Wenyu campaigned south he overcame Xiao Bo and captured Ouyang Yi; most of the plans came from Shancai.
s0055.idiomatic: When Wenyu marched south he defeated Xiao Bo and captured Ouyang Yi; most of the plans were Shancai's.

s0056.literal: When Wenyu marched west against Wang Lin he left Shancai to oversee Jiangzhou affairs and still garrisoned Yuzhang.
s0056.idiomatic: When Wenyu marched west against Wang Lin he left Shancai to oversee Jiangzhou and continued to hold Yuzhang.

s0057.literal: Wenyu with Hou Andu suffered defeat at Dundu; Yu Xiaoxu came from Xinlin to raid Yuzhang; Shancai gathered the remaining troops and attached himself to Zhou Di.
s0057.idiomatic: Wenyu and Hou Andu were beaten at Dundu. Yu Xiaoxu came from Xinlin to strike Yuzhang. Shancai gathered the remnant army and joined Zhou Di.

s0058.literal: Yu Xiaoxu and Li Xiaoqin were captured; Editorial footnote marker 9. Zhou Di sent Shancai by the eastern route from Poyang through the Le'an Ridge to escort them to the capital.
s0058.idiomatic: Zhou Di captured Yu Xiaoxu and Li Xiaoqin; [9] he sent Shancai by the eastern route from Poyang over the Le'an Ridge to deliver them to the capital.

s0059.literal: He was made Regular Attendant of the Secretariat.
s0059.idiomatic: He was made regular attendant of the Secretariat.

s0060.literal: Again by the Le'an Ridge he pacified the commanderies of the southern rivers.
s0060.idiomatic: Again by way of the Le'an Ridge he pacified the southern river commanderies.

s0061.literal: Wenyu again held the Jin Ford of Yuzhang in force; Shancai was again made General of Manifest Prestige, Chief Clerk to the Pacifier of the South, and Administrator of Yuzhang.
s0061.idiomatic: When Wenyu again held the Jin Ford of Yuzhang in force, Shancai was again made general of manifest prestige, chief clerk to the pacifier of the south, and administrator of Yuzhang.

s0062.literal: Wenyu was killed by Xiong Tanlang; Tanlang imprisoned Shancai and the others and sent them to Wang Lin.
s0062.idiomatic: Wenyu was killed by Xiong Tanlang. Tanlang imprisoned Shancai and his party and sent them to Wang Lin.

s0063.literal: Before they arrived, Hou Andu defeated Lin's general Chang Zhong'ai at Gongting Lake, and so Shancai was able to return; he was made General of Manifest Prestige and Administrator of Xin'an.
s0063.idiomatic: Before they arrived, Hou Andu defeated Lin's general Chang Zhong'ai at Gongting Lake, and Shancai was able to return. He was made general of manifest prestige and administrator of Xin'an.

s0064.literal: Because Lin was not yet pacified, he was left to garrison Fuyang to guard the eastern route.
s0064.idiomatic: While Lin was still unbeaten he was left at Fuyang to guard the eastern line.

s0065.literal: He entered court as Supernumerary Regular Attendant and was promoted to Chief Clerk to the Prince of Shixing, Pacifier of the East, conducting office in East Yangzhou.
s0065.idiomatic: He returned to court as supernumerary regular attendant and was promoted to chief clerk to the Prince of Shixing, pacifier of the east, acting in East Yangzhou.

s0066.literal: When Hou Andu campaigned against Liu Yi, Shancai led the princely household troops with him.
s0066.idiomatic: When Hou Andu campaigned against Liu Yi, Shancai led the prince's household troops with him.

s0067.literal: When Yi was pacified, he was made General of Bright Prestige and Administrator of Dongyang.
s0067.idiomatic: After Yi was subdued he was made general of bright prestige and administrator of Dongyang.

s0068.literal: He entered court as Chief Clerk to the Prince of Shixing, Pacifier of the East, concurrently Commandery Assistant of Kuaiji, conducting office in East Yangzhou.
s0068.idiomatic: He returned as chief clerk to the Prince of Shixing, pacifier of the east, with Kuaiji commandery assistant, acting in East Yangzhou.

s0069.literal: Before he took up the appointment he was changed to Regular Attendant, concurrently Acting Master of Revenue; after a full year he received the substantive post.
s0069.idiomatic: Before he entered office he was reassigned to regular attendant and acting master of revenue; after a year he received the substantive appointment.

s0070.literal: Wang Zhi, styled Zizhen, was the younger brother of Right Grand Master of the Golden Sigil Tong.
s0070.idiomatic: Wang Zhi, styled Zizhen, was the younger brother of right grand master of the golden sigil Tong.

s0071.literal: In youth he was bold and generous and ranged widely in books and histories.
s0071.idiomatic: In youth he was bold and generous and read widely in books and histories.

s0072.literal: In Liang times, as Emperor Wu's sister's son he was enfeoffed Marquis of Jiakou ting, entered the National University as student of the Book of Changes, and ranked high in the archery examination.
s0072.idiomatic: Under Liang, as the emperor's sister's son, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Jiakou and studied the Book of Changes at the national university, ranking high in the archery examination.

s0073.literal: He began his career as Secretary, Household Retainer to the Heir Apparent, and Gentleman of the Palace Hall.
s0073.idiomatic: He began as secretary, household retainer to the heir apparent, and gentleman of the palace hall.

s0074.literal: On his mother's death he observed mourning and was known for filial piety.
s0074.idiomatic: When his mother died he mourned her and was known for filial piety.

s0075.literal: When mourning ended he was made Mentor to the Heir Apparent and Leader of Direct Service in the Eastern Palace.
s0075.idiomatic: When mourning ended he was made mentor to the heir apparent and leader of direct service in the eastern palace.

s0076.literal: He rose through Household Retainer and Household Mentor.
s0076.idiomatic: He rose through household retainer and household mentor.

s0077.literal: In the first year of Taiqing he was made Bearer of the Staff and General Who Pacifies the Distance and led the Eastern Palace troops in the Marquis of Zhenyang's northern campaign.
s0077.idiomatic: In the first year of Taiqing (547) he was given the staff as General Who Pacifies the Distance, led the eastern palace troops on the Marquis of Zhenyang's northern campaign.

s0078.literal: When Zhenyang was defeated, Zhi escaped and returned.
s0078.idiomatic: When Zhenyang was beaten, Zhi slipped away and returned.

s0079.literal: When Hou Jing rebelled at Shouyang, Zhi again led the river forces with the massed armies to resist him.
s0079.idiomatic: When Hou Jing rebelled at Shouyang, Zhi again led the river fleet with the allied armies to block him.

s0080.literal: When Jing's army crossed the river, Zhi at once withdrew.
s0080.idiomatic: When Jing's army crossed the Yangzi, Zhi at once fell back.

s0081.literal: Soon he led infantry and cavalry and encamped outside the Xuanyang Gate.
s0081.idiomatic: He soon led foot and horse and encamped outside the Xuanyang Gate.

s0082.literal: When Jing's army reached the capital, Zhi did not fight and his troops collapsed; he then shaved his head as a monk and hid among the people.
s0082.idiomatic: When Jing's army reached the capital, Zhi did not fight; his troops broke and he shaved his head as a monk and hid among the people.

s0083.literal: When Liu Zhongli and the others united to relieve the capital, the army held the south bank; Zhi again gathered the remaining troops and joined them.
s0083.idiomatic: When Liu Zhongli and others united to relieve the capital, their army held the south bank. Zhi again gathered the remnant troops and joined them.

s0084.literal: After the capital fell he fled west to Jingzhou; Emperor Yuan of Liang under the provisional regime made him Right Chief Clerk, concurrently Administrator of Hedong.
s0084.idiomatic: After the capital fell he fled west to Jingzhou. Emperor Yuan of Liang, under the provisional regime, made him right chief clerk and administrator of Hedong.

s0085.literal: Soon he was promoted to Palace Attendant.
s0085.idiomatic: He was soon promoted to palace attendant.

s0086.literal: Soon he went out as Bearer of the Staff, Commander of Military Affairs over Wu province, General Who Pacifies the Distance, and Inspector of Wu, concurrently Interior Magistrate of Poyang.
s0086.idiomatic: He was soon sent out with the staff as commander of military affairs over Wu, General Who Pacifies the Distance, inspector of Wu, and interior magistrate of Poyang.

s0087.literal: When Jing province fell, Hou Tian held Tangcheng and was at odds with Zhi; he sent a subordinate general, Yang Liang, to replace Zhi and also pressed him with troops; Zhi led his command over the Xin'an Ridge and attached himself to Liu Yi.
s0087.idiomatic: When Jing province fell, Hou Tian held Tangcheng and clashed with Zhi. He sent the subordinate general Yang Liang to replace him and advanced with troops. Zhi led his command over the Xin'an Ridge and joined Liu Yi.

s0088.literal: When Emperor Wen garrisoned Kuaiji he sent troops to aid Zhi and had him hold Xin'an county.
s0088.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen held Kuaiji he sent troops to aid Zhi and had him guard Xin'an county.

s0089.literal: In the second year of Yongding the Founder ordered Zhi to lead his command over the ridge into Yuzhang and follow Commander Zhou Wenyu against Wang Lin.
s0089.idiomatic: In the second year of Yongding (558) the Founder ordered Zhi to lead his command over the mountains into Yuzhang and follow Commander Zhou Wenyu against Wang Lin.

s0090.literal: Zhi and Lin had long been on good terms; some slandered him, saying that in the army he secretly corresponded with Lin; the Founder ordered Zhou Wenyu to kill Zhi; Wenyu memorialized to plead for his life, and he was spared.
s0090.idiomatic: Zhi and Lin had long been friends. Some accused him of secret correspondence with Lin in the field. The Founder ordered Zhou Wenyu to execute him; Wenyu pleaded for his life and he was spared.

s0091.literal: Soon he was made Regular Attendant and Administrator of Jinling.
s0091.idiomatic: He was soon made regular attendant and administrator of Jinling.

s0092.literal: When Emperor Wen succeeded he was summoned to hold the Ministry of War.
s0092.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen succeeded he was recalled to head the ministry of war.

s0093.literal: When Emperor Xuan was Inspector of Yangzhou he made Zhi General of Benevolent Prestige and Chief Clerk to the Flying Cavalry.
s0093.idiomatic: When Emperor Xuan was inspector of Yangzhou he made Zhi general of benevolent prestige and chief clerk to the flying cavalry.

s0094.literal: In the second year of Tiancheng he was made Administrator of Jin'an.
s0094.idiomatic: In the second year of Tiancheng (561) he was made administrator of Jin'an.

s0095.literal: When Emperor Xuan served as regent he made Zhi Left Chief Clerk of the Secretariat, general unchanged.
s0095.idiomatic: When Emperor Xuan was regent he made Zhi left chief clerk of the Secretariat, retaining his general's title.

s0096.literal: He was dismissed from office for a public matter.
s0096.idiomatic: He was dismissed for an offense in public business.

s0097.literal: Soon he was made Regular Attendant of Direct Communication, promoted to Grand Steward and Minister of Justice.
s0097.idiomatic: He was soon made regular attendant of direct communication and promoted to grand steward and minister of justice.

s0098.literal: In the second year of Taijian he died, aged sixty.
s0098.idiomatic: In the second year of Taijian (570) he died, aged sixty.

s0099.literal: He was posthumously given his former office; posthumous name Anzi.
s0099.idiomatic: He was posthumously given his former rank, with the posthumous name Anzi.

s0100.literal: Wei Zai, styled Deji, was a native of Duling in Jingzhao.
s0100.idiomatic: Wei Zai, styled Deji, was a native of Duling in Jingzhao.
